claims.text: The starting catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy.
The starting catalyst contains trace platinum-group metals together with Cu, Ni, Pd, and Pt.
ALD can produce a uniform 2–3 nm Ce–Zr oxide coating on the catalyst surface.
The deposited Ce–Zr oxide will form a conformal overlayer that interacts with the alloy surface.
The Ce–Zr overlayer will create active oxygen vacancies.
The Ce–Zr overlayer will physically mitigate catalyst sintering.
The Ce–Zr overlayer will reduce adsorption of poisoning species.
Oxygen-vacancy formation and Ce–Zr redox cycling will promote catalytic oxidation at lower temperatures.
The oxide layer will act as a barrier that protects active sites from poisoning by H2O and NO.
Surface stabilization by the overlayer will maintain catalytic performance during prolonged aging.
Relative to the uncoated catalyst, the coated catalyst will have a lower CO light-off temperature.
Relative to the uncoated catalyst, the coated catalyst will have a lower hydrocarbon-oxidation light-off temperature.
The coated catalyst is expected to enable CO and hydrocarbon oxidation below 150 °C.
The coated catalyst will retain more activity than the uncoated catalyst in the presence of H2O and NO.
The coated catalyst will undergo less degradation than the uncoated catalyst during accelerated aging.
The intervention maintains low platinum-group-metal usage because it adds a Ce–Zr oxide overlayer rather than additional platinum-group metals.
The intervention is anticipated to be effective under regulated automotive exhaust conditions from 150 °C to 600 °C with CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO.
The benefit may be limited under extreme or highly variable conditions beyond typical transient and low-temperature operation.

contradictions.description: The proposed tests cover 150–600 °C, but the predicted and falsifying outcome concerns operation below 150 °C. A test beginning at 150 °C cannot establish a below-150 °C light-off target.
